specPoints.text: understand the interactions in molecules, such as H 2 O, liquid NH 3 and liquid HF, which give rise to hydrogen bonding

understand the following anomalous properties of water resulting from hydrogen bonding: i its high melting and boiling temperature when compared with similar molecules ii the density of ice compared to that of water

primer.text: Water should freeze and boil far lower than it does, yet it stays liquid over a huge range and floats its own ice. The culprit is hydrogen bonding: the strongest pull molecules can feel without a chemical bond. This note catalogs which molecules can form these links, then works through the odd properties that make water unlike every neighbouring hydride.

lessons.title: Molecules that can hydrogen bond
lessons.opening: Hydrogen bonding needs the right structural kit, and several everyday families carry it. This lesson lists the compounds whose O-H, N-H or H-F bonds qualify, and shows why ammonia manages only one link per molecule while water manages two.
keyPoints: Alcohols, ammonia, amines, carboxylic acids, hydrogen fluoride and proteins all carry the required bonds.
Each qualifies because it holds hydrogen attached to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine.
The link forms between that polarised hydrogen and a lone pair on a neighbour's electronegative atom.
Ammonia offers one lone pair on nitrogen, so one molecule forms at most a single hydrogen bond.
Water's oxygen carries two lone pairs, doubling its accepting capacity.

low.restatement: Any molecule holding H on O, N or F can donate a hydrogen bond, and any lone pair on those atoms can accept one; ammonia donates three ways but accepts once.
low.analogy: Each polarised hydrogen is a hook and each lone pair is an eye; ammonia carries three hooks and one eye, water two hooks and two eyes.
low.examPointer: Count lone pairs, not hydrogens, when a question asks how many hydrogen bonds a molecule accepts - ammonia's single nitrogen lone pair caps it at one.

medium.restatement: Donation requires a covalent H-O, H-N or H-F bond whose hydrogen carries heavy positive character; acceptance requires a lone pair localised on O, N or F, so ammonia's accepting count is one and water's is two.
medium.analogy: A three-legged stool needs one solid floor point (the lone pair) to complete each contact; more floors let more stools cluster, which is exactly water's advantage.
medium.examPointer: For 'which compounds hydrogen bond' items, scan the formula for H on O, N or F - ethanol passes, ethane fails, and saying 'any polar molecule' loses the mark.

check.stem: Which compound from the list hydrogen bonds through an N-H bond?

options.text: Ammonia
options.explanation: Ammonia's three N-H bonds make it a hydrogen-bond donor.

options.text: Ethane
options.explanation: Ethane carries only C-H bonds, which never hydrogen bond.

options.text: Sodium chloride
options.explanation: An ionic solid has no covalent H-N bond at all.

options.text: Tetrachloromethane
options.explanation: Its C-Cl bonds leave the hydrogens absent entirely.

check.stem: Why can one ammonia molecule form at most one hydrogen bond as an acceptor?

options.text: Nitrogen holds a single lone pair
options.explanation: One lone pair means one accepting site, whatever the donor count.

options.text: Its three hydrogens fill all sites
options.explanation: Donor hydrogens do not consume the lone pair that accepts.

options.text: Ammonia is non-polar
options.explanation: Ammonia is polar and hydrogen bonds strongly.

options.text: Its H-N bonds are too weak
options.explanation: The bonds are strong; the accepting capacity is the limiter.

check.stem: Which statement about hydrogen-bond donors is correct?

options.text: The hydrogen must be covalently bonded to O, N or F
options.explanation: Only these partners polarise hydrogen enough to donate.

options.text: Any hydrogen in the molecule can donate
options.explanation: C-H hydrogens lack the positive character required.

options.text: The hydrogen must carry a full positive charge
options.explanation: Partial positive character, not a full charge, does the work.

options.text: Donation needs a metal cation nearby
options.explanation: Metal cations play no role in hydrogen bonding.

check.stem: Proteins hydrogen bond internally. Which bond type in a protein does the work?

options.text: N-H bonds in the amide groups
options.explanation: Protein backbones carry N-H bonds that reach carbonyl oxygens.

options.text: C-C bonds along the chain
options.explanation: Carbon-carbon bonds never hydrogen bond.

options.text: C-H bonds on side groups
options.explanation: C-H bonds are never hydrogen-bond donors.

options.text: Ionic links between residues
options.explanation: The question asks about hydrogen bonding, not salt bridges.

check.stem: Water accepts two hydrogen bonds per molecule because its oxygen has:

options.text: Two lone pairs
options.explanation: Both lone pairs can face donor hydrogens simultaneously.

options.text: Two covalent bonds to hydrogen
options.explanation: The O-H bonds make it a donor; acceptance is the lone pairs' job.

options.text: A double bond to oxygen
options.explanation: Water's oxygen bonds to hydrogens only.

options.text: A negative formal charge
options.explanation: Water is neutral overall.

check.stem: List four compound classes that can form hydrogen bonds.
check.modelAnswer: Alcohols, ammonia, amines, carboxylic acids, hydrogen fluoride and proteins all qualify - any four of these answer the question.

check.stem: State how many hydrogen bonds one molecule of ammonia can form in total and why.
check.modelAnswer: Ammonia tops out at one hydrogen bond per molecule, because its nitrogen presents only a single lone pair as an accepting site.

check.stem: Explain why hydrogen fluoride and water both hydrogen bond but hydrogen sulfide barely does.
check.modelAnswer: Fluorine and oxygen are the most electronegative atoms that bond to hydrogen, so they drain enough density to expose hydrogen strongly; sulfur is far less electronegative, so its H-S bonds leave hydrogen barely positive and no real hydrogen bonding forms.

check.stem: A molecule carries three donor hydrogens and one lone pair. If each completed hydrogen bond stores 20 kJ per mole, what is the maximum accepting energy per mole of contacts through the lone pair?
check.modelAnswer: The single lone pair accepts only one contact, so the accepting side stores just 20 kJ per mole however many donor hydrogens dangle unused.

lessons.title: Water's anomalous melting and boiling
lessons.opening: Water melts and boils far above the values its size predicts. This lesson attributes the anomaly to hydrogen bonding in both ice and liquid water, then reads the hydride graph where water's vaporisation enthalpy triples the trend line.
keyPoints: Water melts and boil high because hydrogen bonds run through both ice and liquid water.
Separating water molecules therefore costs much more energy than size alone predicts.
Across the Group 16 hydrides the vaporisation enthalpy climbs from H2S toward H2Te as electrons accumulate.
Electron counting would put water near 17 kJ per mole on the trend line.
Hydrogen bonding lifts water's actual value to almost three times that figure.

low.restatement: Hydrogen bonds tie water molecules together so tightly that melting and boiling need unusually high temperatures, and the vaporisation enthalpy lands far above the hydride trend.
low.analogy: Water molecules hold hands across the whole room while H2S neighbours merely brush shoulders - the hand-holding crowd needs a much louder signal (more heat) to disperse.
low.examPointer: Quote both halves of the argument: the trend prediction from electron count, then the hydrogen-bond premium - one half alone scores half the marks.

medium.restatement: Descending Group 16, growing electron counts strengthen induced dipole contributions and raise vaporisation enthalpy smoothly; water sits off that smooth line because its extra energy is spent snapping hydrogen bonds rather than only induced attractions.
medium.analogy: Three rungs of a ladder rise steadily, but the fourth rung (water) is bolted three times higher because a hidden brace (hydrogen bonding) holds it there.
medium.examPointer: State the direction of the comparison precisely - water's value is larger than the extrapolated trend, not smaller - and name hydrogen bonds as the cause.

check.stem: Why does water boil far higher than its molecular size suggests?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds must be broken on top of the usual attractions
options.explanation: The extra energy bill for hydrogen bonding lifts the boiling point.

options.text: Water's covalent bonds break at boiling
options.explanation: Boiling separates molecules without touching covalent bonds.

options.text: Water has an unusually large electron count
options.explanation: Water's electrons sit below the heavier hydrides, not above.

options.text: Steam is ionic
options.explanation: Steam remains molecular water.

check.stem: Along the trend from H2S to H2Te, vaporisation enthalpy increases because:

options.text: Heavier Group 16 hydrides carry more electrons, strengthening induced forces
options.explanation: Growing electron clouds raise the induced-dipole contribution down the group.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding strengthens down the group
options.explanation: H2S, H2Se and H2Te barely hydrogen bond at all.

options.text: The molecules become lighter
options.explanation: They become heavier down the group.

options.text: Metallic character grows
options.explanation: No metal character appears in these hydrides.

check.stem: Roughly where does electron counting place water's expected vaporisation enthalpy, and where does it actually sit?

options.text: Predicted near 17 kJ per mole, actually almost three times larger
options.explanation: The trend extrapolation gives about 17, and hydrogen bonding triples it.

options.text: Predicted near 17 kJ per mole, actually about half
options.explanation: Water sits above the trend, not below it.

options.text: Predicted near 170 kJ per mole, actually lower
options.explanation: Both figures are an order of magnitude off.

options.text: Prediction and reality coincide
options.explanation: The anomaly is the entire point of the graph.

check.stem: What must be supplied to melt ice beyond what a typical small molecule needs?

options.text: Energy to loosen the hydrogen-bonded open lattice
options.explanation: Melting weakens the hydrogen-bond framework holding ice together.

options.text: Energy to break O-H covalent bonds
options.explanation: Covalent bonds survive melting intact.

options.text: Energy to ionise the molecules
options.explanation: No ionisation occurs during melting.

options.text: Nothing beyond induced forces
options.explanation: That would make ice melt near H2S's values.

check.stem: Which phrase best describes the cause of water's anomalous properties?

options.text: Extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules
options.explanation: Every anomaly in this note traces back to hydrogen bonding.

options.text: High molar mass of water
options.explanation: Water is lighter than its Group 16 neighbours.

options.text: Ionic character inside water
options.explanation: Water is covalently bonded throughout.

options.text: Weak induced forces in water
options.explanation: Weak induced forces would lower, not raise, the boiling point.

check.stem: State the two states of water in which hydrogen bonding must be overcome to melt and to boil it.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding holds both ice (solid water) and liquid water, so the strong intermolecular framework must be overcome for melting and for boiling.

check.stem: Quote the approximate trend-line value for water's vaporisation enthalpy and the size of the observed premium.
check.modelAnswer: Electron counting predicts around 17 kJ per mole, and hydrogen bonding pushes the observed value to almost three times that figure.

check.stem: Explain why the hydride graph would mislead a student who ignored hydrogen bonding.
check.modelAnswer: Reading only electron counts, the student would extrapolate water below H2S and predict a low vaporisation enthalpy; the actual value towers above the line because hydrogen bonds add an energy channel the trend never contains.

check.stem: If the hydride trend predicts 17 kJ per mole for water and the observed premium factor is 3, estimate water's vaporisation enthalpy and the size of the hydrogen-bond premium alone.
check.modelAnswer: Three times 17 kJ per mole gives about 51 kJ per mole, so the hydrogen-bond premium contributes roughly 34 kJ per mole beyond the trend.

lessons.title: Surface tension and the density anomaly
lessons.opening: Two more water oddities complete the set. This lesson explains how surface molecules, pulled inward by hydrogen bonds, build the skin that insects skate on, and why ice's open lattice leaves it floating nine percent lighter than the liquid below.
keyPoints: Surface tension is a liquid surface resisting external force.
Surface water molecules are hydrogen bonded to neighbours below and beside them, pulling them inward.
That inward pull compresses the surface layer and raises its tension.
Most solids pack denser than their liquids, but ice locks molecules into an open lattice.
The open lattice and long hydrogen-bond lengths leave ice about nine percent less dense than liquid water.

low.restatement: Molecules at the surface lose the neighbours above them, so the hydrogen bonds tug them inward and tighten the skin; freezing locks water into a spread-out lattice whose molecules sit further apart, so ice floats.
low.analogy: A crowd at a fence: people inside push and pull every which way, but those at the barrier are dragged backward by friends behind them, so the front line packs tight.
low.examPointer: Quote the figure 'about nine percent' when asked how much less dense ice is - precise numbers earn the mark.

medium.restatement: Unbalanced hydrogen bonding at the interface produces a net inward force raising surface tension; on freezing, the tetrahedral hydrogen-bond geometry fixes an open framework whose bond lengths spread molecules further apart than the disordered liquid achieves.
medium.analogy: Scaffolding built with rigid corner braces spans more space than the same poles dumped loosely in a pile - the braced frame is the ice, the loose pile the liquid.
medium.examPointer: Link cause to effect in one chain: hydrogen bonds, open lattice, longer separations, lower density - skipping a link costs the explanation mark.

check.stem: What is surface tension?

options.text: A liquid surface's capacity to resist external forces
options.explanation: That resistance comes from the inward hydrogen-bond pull on surface molecules.

options.text: The weight of a liquid column
options.explanation: Weight is gravity's effect, not surface behaviour.

options.text: The pressure inside a liquid drop
options.explanation: Internal pressure is a different quantity.

options.text: The rate of evaporation from a surface
options.explanation: Evaporation rate is unrelated to tension here.

check.stem: Why are surface water molecules pulled downward?

options.text: Hydrogen bonds to neighbours below and beside them drag them inward
options.explanation: Missing neighbours above leave an unbalanced inward force.

options.text: Air pressure squeezes them down
options.explanation: Air pressure acts uniformly, not as the molecular mechanism.

options.text: Gravity attracts only surface molecules
options.explanation: Gravity acts on all molecules equally.

options.text: Their covalent bonds stretch downward
options.explanation: Covalent bonds stay internal to each molecule.

check.stem: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: Ice's open hydrogen-bonded lattice leaves it about nine percent less dense
options.explanation: The spread-out solid structure drops below the liquid's density.

options.text: Ice has fewer electrons than water
options.explanation: Freezing changes no electron count.

options.text: Liquid water loses hydrogen bonds entirely
options.explanation: Liquid water keeps a hydrogen-bonded network, just less ordered.

options.text: Air trapped inside ice lowers its mass
options.explanation: The density gap is structural, not trapped air.

check.stem: Which statement compares packing in ice and liquid water?

options.text: Ice molecules sit slightly further apart because of the open lattice and long hydrogen-bond lengths
options.explanation: Both factors spread the solid structure.

options.text: Ice packs molecules more tightly than the liquid
options.explanation: That is true of most substances but not water.

options.text: Both states pack identically
options.explanation: Identical packing would give equal densities and no floating.

options.text: Liquid water packs in an open lattice
options.explanation: The open lattice belongs to ice.

check.stem: Which everyday observation follows from water's high surface tension?

options.text: Insects skating on pond water
options.explanation: The tensioned skin supports light loads from above.

options.text: Salt dissolving rapidly
options.explanation: Dissolution is a solvation story, not a tension one.

options.text: Ice sinking in drinks
options.explanation: Ice floats, the opposite.

options.text: Water boiling at 100 degrees
options.explanation: Boiling point is the earlier anomaly, not tension.

check.stem: State the density relationship between ice and liquid water, with the percentage.
check.modelAnswer: Ice is about nine percent less dense than liquid water, because its open hydrogen-bonded lattice spreads the molecules further apart.

check.stem: Define surface tension in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: Surface tension is a liquid surface's capacity to resist any external force pressing on it, produced by the inward pull on surface molecules.

check.stem: Explain why the molecules at a liquid surface experience a net inward pull.
check.modelAnswer: A surface molecule has hydrogen-bonded neighbours beside and below it but none above, so the attractions it feels no longer cancel in all directions and their sum points into the liquid.

check.stem: Ice is nine percent less dense than liquid water. If liquid water's density is 1.00 g per cubic centimetre, estimate ice's density.
check.modelAnswer: Nine percent below 1.00 gives about 0.91 g per cubic centimetre, the figure that keeps icebergs riding high.

glossary.definition: The strongest intermolecular attraction, running from a hydrogen bonded to O, N or F to a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
The unusual behaviours of water that hydrogen bonding produces: melting and boiling far above expectations, a tense surface skin, and ice that floats.
The energy required to vaporise one mole of a liquid, which water raises far above its hydride trend line.
A liquid surface's capacity to resist external forces, produced by the unbalanced inward pull on its molecules.
